problem: Visual navigation agents such as image-goal navigation agents need a memory of their navigation history. Existing memories are either unstructured recurrent states or metric/topological maps that rely on labels, poses or hand-designed features. The paper targets the lack of a compact, structured memory built only from self-supervised image representations.
motivation: Image-goal navigation needs the agent to recall where it has been and relate that history to the goal image. A graph whose nodes are visually distinct places is a natural, scalable way to store this. The paper's observation is that representations learned without labels, from unlabeled images, can be compared by similarity to decide when an observation is a new place. That lets the agent build a topological memory incrementally while it navigates, with no supervision on node identity.
key_idea: Incrementally build a visual graph memory (VGM) whose nodes are unsupervised image embeddings, adding or linking nodes by embedding similarity, and let the navigation policy read it with a graph convolutional network plus attention conditioned on the goal and the current observation.
insight: The abstract claims that a graph memory keyed on unsupervised embedding similarity can hold both the navigation history and task-related information (e.g., goal relevance), and that this beats state-of-the-art image-goal navigation methods on Gibson. It attributes the gain to the combination of structured graph memory, GCN message passing and attention-based memory reading. Specific ablations such as memory vs. no memory, or unsupervised vs. supervised features, are not visible in the abstract, so which component matters most cannot be confirmed from this text.
method: Unsupervised image representation: an image encoder is pre-trained on an unlabeled image dataset without labels, giving embeddings used both as graph node features and for the similarity comparisons.

Incremental VGM construction: at each step the current observation's embedding is compared with existing nodes by similarity. A sufficiently novel observation becomes a new node connected to the previous node; otherwise the agent is localized to an existing node. The graph therefore grows along the navigation history.
Graph encoding: a graph convolutional network propagates information over VGM nodes and edges. The node features can carry task information such as the goal embedding.
Attention-based memory read-out: attention with the current observation and goal as queries over the GCN-encoded node features produces a memory context vector.

Policy: the memory context plus current observation and goal features feed an action policy that navigates while simultaneously building the VGM. Training details (imitation vs. RL) are not given in the abstract.
